children.author: drewg123
children.text:
Its a spectrum. For ai-maintained code (like a gui to visualize performance data), IDGAF what the code looks like. I just let claude or codex go nuts and 100% vibe code.

For code I care about, I audit every single hunk as its produced. I give it extensive style guidelines, and crack down on things like a 20-line essay in a comment.

For mission critical code, I write the code myself and have an agent review it.

children.author: drgo
children.text: The way I have been doing it is to use LLMs to generate the code that I don't want to write: prototypes, tests, benchmarks, isolated,straightforward almost copy-paste code. I still write my own code as before because I enjoy doing that and because trying to understand and fix what an LLM generates and regenerates is harder and more tedious and time consuming than writing the code the way I want to do it in the first place.

children.author: tmarice
children.text:
After vibing myself into a corner multiple times on important projects, I now have only two modes: clankermaxx for code I don't really care about (mostly frontend react), and write by hand everything else. Using Django for backend already removes the most of the cruft, and writing by hand also means I actually understand what's going on. Works fine for now.

I'm still on the fence for tests: I don't really like to write them, but the LLM-generated tests are pretty bad, even the frontier models on xhigh thinking. I usually generate them, but I don't really have the confidence they test anything except 1==1. Unfortunately it's hard to justify the time spent on writing them manually.

children.text:
My experience as well. Opus 5.5 is really good at matching the existing coding style. I often look at code and think I wrote it, only to realize it was written by Opus.

The trick is to give it enough guidance about the style you prefer.

I generally produce nearly the same code I'd write myself about 5x faster with AI. I don't just let Claude Code run wild for a long time and have a mess to review. I have it do small chunks I can quickly review, give it feedback, iterate, etc until I like the output, then I move on to the next step. This takes time of course but I've found it faster than reviewing a giant mess of a code review.

I try to have a good overall idea of what I want to build from the start. Sometimes I don't know and that involves long walks and iterative conversations with the agents. It's okay to stub out functionality or modules and the agent will be comfortable with this. As the agent builds, I have it update an architecture document.

It's always good to have another agent (sans existing context) review the project for slop and hacks, best practices, security flaws, etc. I usually have Codex do one, and Claude do the other. Hope this makes sense.

Agree, you can't spec what you don't know yet. Two things could help:
Let the agent grill you before writing the spec. Answering its questions surfaces a lot of the unknowns.
Then have a different model grill the plan, with questions specific to your product. In one case of mine, that caught a design issue which the generic review missed.

> Write good specs into files, usually Markdown.

When I'm building something new there's a good chance I don't know about a lot of problems (unknown unknowns). How do you overcome this with just spec files?

I keep coming back to this and the only way to develop properly without tons of hacks patching bugs afterwards is by working at a low level. I don't really write code but I work at the code level still and have Claude write each function and whatnot.

We have multiple apps, but I'll share only the free ones; the others are B2B (they haul in major revenue for us, and businesses dealing with us will not like us disclosing this here), largest free one is MacroCodex with 17,000+ users.

We do not have this problem; we heavily use the models from OpenAI and Anthropic, but we have a custom harness built for ultimate cache efficiency and a purpose tuned workflow.

Codex is GREAT but it keeps updating and its UI changes often (remember mini git sidebar ui?)

Our Custom Harness does multiple things, like having a "Skill Selector," which uses our Gambler v1 (26B decision model responds in <100ms locally) and overlays tools on top of existing ones (as the models are RLVL over the specific tool in their harness, we overlay those tools with a familiar interface or format and inject custom features we want the model to interpret). Other than this, it leverages local models to accelerate development. Also, instead of providing custom tools, we actually use the same tools that their original model-provided harness uses. We've a list of 100s of such optimizations; these are just a few from the top of my head.

I have been working on harnesses for a very long time; I read research papers and implement them.

The apps use Flutter and Rust for all of our apps; no ads, no subscriptions.

So, macrocodex is basically a neural network product which "predicts" maintenance calories at a very high accuracy, https://macrocodex.app/

MacroCodex beats everything in its category and it does it for free, no ads, no subscriptions.

Symbiote and CalorieCodex will soon follow the suite.

If it fails, people get fat instead of losing weight, or get skinny instead of gaining weight.

Recently, we launched CalorieCodex (a calorie tracking app with an optional Full Agent Harness, where an agent tracks calories for you) and Symbiote (a programmable workout app; think BoostCamp, but user-programmable so it can run any bodybuilding program).

You can find some screenshots here: https://macrocodex.app/guides/peak-week/

children.author: saluki
children.text:
Having great success with Claude Code.

Short claude.md file, skills for various things like db schema, etc

For larger or complex features do a design session with claude, review design and make suggestions and collaborate, once design is dialed in ask to break in to tasks then do similar session collaboarating on plan.md files for each task/phase then have claude build it.

Claude is really really good at adding tests, leverage this for near 100% test coverage and it can also test that it's meeting the PRD/spec.

It's also creative and seems to like collaborating on the design and plan parts join in with that. Claude feels really similar to my favorite engineer I worked with as far as collaboration and even banter. It's nice.

Using claude code in the terminal btw, md files go in repo so all team, devs, consoles can see context across front and backend.

Use PRs run claude code review, I created a Minority Report style review skill as well, code quality, security, performance with anderton as the judge/orch

Then we have a human review PR as well

This process we are getting good code and faster velocity for sure, vs traditional SDLC for solo and with team

As far as reading the code, I think that will become less and less as long as it passes automated code review, it's performant, meets the spec and tests pass . . . SHIP IT

Watch DHH's recent RailsConf keynote, this is where we're heading, buckle up

children.author: kittomic
children.text:
I think if you’re human-reviewing all the output of AI, then you’re going to hit the human comprehension bottleneck.

The key is to have clear specs and clear architecture, and then have agents enforce this.

I devote most of my time to specs and much more of my time to e2e and integration tests.

I find a lot of value, even more value than before, in strictly hexagonal designs and even a large does of DDD.

Following these principles, it’s relatively easy to design systems of systems that decompose to domains that decompose into use cases / ports / adapters.

By the time you’ve decomposed to this level, AI is very capable and it’s easy to review or verify by tests. I am very comfortable with AI verifying if a basic CRUD port is functional, for example, because at this point each operation becomes less than a dozen lines of code.

Stop thinking of yourself as a programmer and start thinking of yourself as an architect.

The key rule is that decomposition of a problem into smaller problems is what wins. This was always true, extremely true before AI and extremely true with AI.

Focus your individual effort on the top-level decompositions and let AI handle the lower-level decompositions. Trust AI to test the lower-level and make sure you test the higher levels.
